body:
A Spanish land grant, generations before American settlement

Holly Hill's land history predates American Florida by decades. In the early 1800s, Governor Coppinger of Spanish East Florida granted 4,500 acres along the Halifax River to Fernando de la Maza Arredondo, part of the same wave of Spanish colonial land grants that shaped much of early Florida land ownership before the territory ever became a state.

Named for an Irish home, not a Florida tree

American settlement began in 1876, when William Samuel Fleming Sr. settled the area and gave it its name. Fleming named the town Holly Hill because it reminded him of his home in Ireland, known as Hollywood, not because of any particular abundance of holly trees on the land itself, a detail that surprises most people who assume the name is purely botanical. The town incorporated on July 1, 1901, and its original purpose was almost comically practical rather than civic-minded in the usual sense: the incorporation was passed specifically to force local owners of razorback hogs to keep their livestock penned up, a genuine, documented piece of small-town Florida history.

The yacht builder who became a Prohibition legend

Holly Hill's most famous resident by far is Bill McCoy. The McCoy family moved to Holly Hill around 1900, and Bill and his brother Ben became accomplished boat builders, running a marina where 11th Street, now LPGA Boulevard, meets the Halifax River. By 1918, McCoy had built a real reputation as a skilled yacht builder, constructing vessels for wealthy clients including Andrew Carnegie and the Vanderbilts. When the automobile began replacing boat travel as the preferred way to get around, that business slowed, and when Prohibition took effect in 1920, McCoy and his brother made a consequential decision: they sold their boat-building assets, traveled to Gloucester, Massachusetts, bought a schooner, and went into rum running.

Why they called it "the real McCoy"

McCoy renamed his ship Tomoka, after the river that runs through his hometown of Holly Hill, a small, genuine detail that ties the whole story back to this exact town. His rum-running shipments became highly prized because, unlike many other smugglers of the era, he refused to cut or water down his liquor. That reputation for honest, uncut product is the popular explanation for how the phrase "the real McCoy" entered the language, though the phrase's true origin is genuinely disputed among etymologists, other rum runners and even older uses of the phrase have their own claims. What isn't disputed is that Bill McCoy was a real, documented Holly Hill resident and one of the most famous rum runners in American history.

What that history means for real estate today

Holly Hill sits on the western shoreline of the Halifax River between Daytona Beach and Ormond Beach, and its real history, a Spanish land grant, an oddly specific hog-pen incorporation, and a genuine national Prohibition legend, gives the town a real identity distinct from being treated as just a pass-through between its two larger neighbors. The Holly Hill History Museum keeps that story visible locally. For an agent, being able to tell a buyer the real story behind a town this small is a genuine differentiator, and Holly Hill's story is a better one than most.

faq.q: Why is Holly Hill, Florida called Holly Hill?
faq.a: William Samuel Fleming Sr., who settled the area in 1876, named it Holly Hill because it reminded him of his home in Ireland, called Hollywood, not because of holly trees growing locally.

faq.q: Why did Holly Hill incorporate as a city?
faq.a: Holly Hill incorporated on July 1, 1901. Its original stated purpose was to force local owners of razorback hogs to keep their livestock penned up, a genuinely documented, practical civic reason rather than a broader governance ambition.

faq.q: Who was Bill McCoy and what is his connection to Holly Hill?
faq.a: Bill McCoy was a Holly Hill yacht builder, based at a marina on the Halifax River, who built boats for clients including Andrew Carnegie and the Vanderbilts before becoming a famous Prohibition-era rum runner known for never watering down his liquor.

faq.q: Did the phrase "the real McCoy" come from Holly Hill?
faq.a: Bill McCoy of Holly Hill is a popular, commonly cited source for the phrase, tied to his reputation for honest, uncut rum-running liquor during Prohibition. The phrase's true origin is genuinely disputed among historians and etymologists, with other rival claims.
